paragraphs.heading: A telescope as wide as Earth
paragraphs.text: The Event Horizon Telescope (EHT) links radio telescopes around the world into one array. It uses very-long-baseline interferometry (VLBI), in which antennas hundreds or thousands of kilometres apart work together as one virtual telescope as wide as the planet. That gives it fine enough detail to see an object as small as the event horizon of a supermassive black hole.

paragraphs.heading: Targets and team
paragraphs.text: Its targets include the two black holes that look largest from Earth. One sits at the center of Messier 87, a supergiant elliptical galaxy; the other is Sagittarius A*, at the center of the Milky Way. The collaboration was launched in 2009 and now has over 300 members from 60 institutions in more than 20 countries and regions.

paragraphs.heading: How the data travel
paragraphs.text: Each antenna has an extremely precise atomic clock. Its signals are turned into digital data and stored on hard drives together with the clock's timing. Commercial cargo planes fly the drives to MIT's Haystack Observatory and to the Max Planck Institute for Radio Astronomy, where they are combined and analysed. With the 2017 data, the full set had to wait until December, because no flights go in or out of the South Pole in the southern winter.

paragraphs.heading: The first black hole image
paragraphs.text: On April 10, 2019, the collaboration released the first image of a black hole, the one at the center of Messier 87, known as M87*. It was announced at six press conferences around the world at the same time and described in six scientific papers. The observation was made at a wavelength of 1.3 mm. In May 2022 astronomers unveiled the first image of Sagittarius A*.

paragraphs.heading: Testing Einstein
paragraphs.text: The image tested Einstein's general theory of relativity under extreme conditions. Relativity predicts a dark, shadow-like region caused by light being bent and captured, and the image matched it. It also gave a mass of 6.5±0.7 billion solar masses and an event horizon about 40 billion kilometres across. That is roughly 2.5 times smaller than the shadow it casts.

paragraphs.heading: Checking the picture
paragraphs.text: Turning data from many radio telescopes into a picture takes a lot of mathematics. To judge how reliable the result was, four separate teams made images. The methods finally used were CLEAN, an established image-building algorithm in radio astronomy, and a regularized maximum likelihood (RML) algorithm.
